chapter.title: Writing a brief the builder can't misread

cards.body:
Tell a contractor 'make the kitchen nice' and you get *their* idea of nice: an island you trip over, a tap you never asked for. Tell them 'two cooks, one long counter, sink under the window, no island' and they can start today.

**A brief is a short note the builder can't misread.** With Claude Code, the note is the request you type.
cards.simpler: Say to a builder 'make the kitchen nice' and you get their idea of nice. Maybe an island you keep bumping into. Maybe a tap you never wanted. Say instead 'two cooks, one long counter, sink under the window, no island' and they can start today. **A brief is a short note the builder can't misread.** With Claude Code, that note is the request you type.

cards.prompt: You leave a note on the counter for your builder before heading out. Which note gets you the kitchen you actually pictured?

options.text: Make it nice. You've seen my place, you know my taste.
For two people who cook every night. One long counter, sink under the window, no island. Done when I can wash a pan and see the garden.
Four pages on my childhood kitchen, every oven brand I've ever liked, and a sketch of my dream house.

whyNot.a: That's trust, not a brief: the builder still has to guess who cooks, how many, and what 'nice' means to you.
whyNot.c: That's a memoir, not a brief: the one thing you want is buried under 40 things you don't.

cards.reteach: A good brief says who it's for, the one job, and what done looks like, in a few lines. Too little and the builder guesses. Too much and the builder picks the wrong thing to focus on. Short and specific wins.

cards.title: Who, and the one job
cards.body:
A brief has 4 parts. The first two: *who it's for* and *the one job* it does. 'A page for me, on my phone, where I add a task and tick it off.' That is already better than most first requests.

Claude Code fills every gap you leave with a guess. Leave out the user, it guesses an app for the whole internet. Leave out the job, it guesses 5 jobs. **Every gap is a guess you'll spend a message undoing.**

Say 'one job' and mean it. If you can't say the job in one sentence, you have two apps.
cards.simpler: A brief has 4 parts. The first two are who it's for and the one job it does. 'A page for me, on my phone, where I add a task and tick it off.' That already beats most first tries. Claude Code fills every gap you leave with a guess. Skip the user, it guesses an app for the whole internet. Skip the job, it guesses 5 jobs. **Every gap is a guess you'll spend a message undoing.** If the job won't fit in one sentence, you have two apps.

cards.title: Priya's recipe app, twice
cards.body:
Priya types: 'make me a recipe app.' Claude builds 4 pages, a search bar, star ratings and a sign-in screen. She can't sign in to her own app, because no account exists yet.

Second try, 5 lines: 'For me only. One page listing my 6 go-to dinners so I stop ordering takeout on Tuesdays. Each dinner: name and a 1-line note. Done when I open it on my phone and see all 6. No sign-in, no search, one file.'

**It works on the first run.** It is also, she admits, the first app she's owned with fewer features than her fridge.
cards.simpler: Priya types 'make me a recipe app.' Claude builds 4 pages, a search bar, star ratings and a sign-in screen. She can't sign in to her own app, because no account exists yet. Second try, 5 lines: 'For me only. One page listing my 6 go-to dinners so I stop ordering takeout on Tuesdays. Each dinner: name and a 1-line note. Done when I open it on my phone and see all 6. No sign-in, no search, one file.' **It works on the first run.** She admits it has fewer features than her fridge.

cards.prompt: Your flatmate Sam wants a page to split the dinner bill 3 ways. Which request applies the brief idea?

options.text: Build a bill-splitting app. Make it clean and modern, with whatever features bill apps usually have.
For 3 flatmates. One job: type the total, see what each person owes. Done when I type 60 and see 20 three times. No sign-in, no history, one file.
For 3 flatmates. Split the bill, track who paid last month, send reminders, show a chart, and let guests join.

whyNot.a: That's 'make it nice' again: no user, no single job, and 'whatever features' invites the builder's guesses.
whyNot.c: That's 5 jobs, not one: splitting, history, reminders, charts and guests are at least 3 apps.

cards.reteach: The brief names who, one job, what done looks like, and what to leave out. 'Type 60, see 20 three times' is something you can check by looking. That's the test of a good done line.

cards.title: Done when, and leave out
cards.body:
Parts 3 and 4: *done when* and *leave out*. 'Done when' is one sentence you can check by looking: 'I type 60 and see 20 three times.' Not 'it works well'. If you can't picture checking it, Claude can't either.

'Leave out' names what the builder adds by habit: sign-in, a database, a fancy design, extra pages. **Say no to those out loud** and the first version stays small enough to test in 2 minutes.

Put the 4 parts in 5 lines or fewer. The fifth line is for how it should be built, if you care: 'one file, plain HTML'. If you don't know yet, skip it.
cards.simpler: Parts 3 and 4 are done when and leave out. 'Done when' is one sentence you can check by looking. 'I type 60 and see 20 three times.' Not 'it works well'. If you can't picture checking it, Claude can't either. 'Leave out' names what a builder adds by habit: sign-in, a database, a fancy design, extra pages. **Say no to those out loud** so the first version stays small enough to test in 2 minutes. Keep the 4 parts to 5 lines or fewer. The fifth line is for how to build it, like 'one file, plain HTML'. Not sure yet? Skip it.

cards.body:
Dev writes a perfect 5-line brief for a water-tracking page, then adds a sixth line: 'and also make it look professional, add anything else you think is useful.' Claude adds a settings page, dark mode and a weekly chart. The one job, tapping a glass, now sits behind 2 menus.

**Spot it by the words 'also' and 'anything'** at the end of a request. That's the door you just opened for guesses.
cards.simpler: Dev writes a perfect 5-line brief for a water-tracking page. Then adds a sixth line: 'and also make it look professional, add anything else you think is useful.' Claude adds a settings page, dark mode and a weekly chart. The one job, tapping a glass, now hides behind 2 menus. **Spot it by the words 'also' and 'anything'** at the end of a request. Those words are the door you just opened for guesses.

cards.prompt: A friend shows you their brief: 'For me. One job: log my 10-minute walks. No sign-in, no map, one file.' It's close. Which part is missing?

options.text: The user: it never says who the app is for.
The done-when line: nothing you can check by looking.
The leave-out line: it never says what not to build.

whyNot.a: 'For me' is the user, so that part is there.
whyNot.c: 'No sign-in, no map, one file' is the leave-out part, so that one's there too.

cards.reteach: Four parts: who, one job, done when, leave out. Your friend has three. Add one line you can check by eye: 'Done when I tap a button and see today's count go up by 1.'

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **A brief is 5 lines or fewer**: who it's for, the one job, what done looks like by eye, and what to leave out. Every line you skip, Claude fills with a guess you'll have to undo.
cards.simpler: **A brief is 5 lines or fewer.** Say who it's for. Say the one job it does. Say what done looks like, in a way you can check by eye. Say what to leave out. Every line you skip, Claude fills with a guess, and you'll have to undo that guess later. Think of it like a shopping list: the shorter and clearer it is, the less chance of coming home with the wrong thing.

cards.body: Open Claude Code in an empty folder. Type a 5-line brief for one page you'd actually use this week. Count the lines before you press enter. If there's an 'also', delete it.
cards.simpler: Open Claude Code in an empty folder. Type a 5-line brief for one page you'd actually use this week. Say who it's for, the one job, what done looks like, and what to leave out. **Count the lines before you press enter.** If one of them has an 'also' in it, delete that part. A short, clear note gets you a first version you can test today.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a 5-line brief, with who, one job, done when and leave out, and get a working first version without going back and forth more than twice.
